read_first: docs/vedant.md for the design decisions and traps; docs/world_model.md for the proxy baseline and acceptance criteria
you_are_the_objective: Blocks 7, 8 and 9 exist to build your input. The system is judged by how quickly and correctly you identify attacks and state over your rollout, not by per-flow scores. If a representation change helps you and hurts per-flow numbers, that is a trade to make - say so.

files.latents_manifest.json: read first: day, n_events, event_latent_dim, arm, observation_budget_ms, ordering, endpoint semantics
files.event_latents.parquet: one row per event with packets, in availability order

input.ordering: sorted by (t_obs, event_id) - the order Block 8 processed them in. An event does not exist before its observation time.

columns.t: float64 epoch seconds, the flow's first packet
columns.t_obs: float64 epoch seconds, when the verdict was available (10 ms after t, or flow end if sooner)
columns.sender_node_id: int32, host that sent the flow's FIRST packet
columns.dt_src: float32 seconds since that sender's previous event
columns.dt_dst: float32 seconds since that receiver's previous event
columns.reversed: bool, the flow record's src/dst disagree with first-packet direction
columns.z: float32[32] Block 9's latent - the compression of Block 8's context. YOUR INPUT.
columns.recon_error: float32, Block 9's reconstruction error on the benign scale. Available, unused by the proxy.
columns.label: string family name, or Benign

warnings: split == -1 are 120 s embargo rows between segments. WALK them to build state, never score or train on them.
Splits are ordered in time: train < val < test. Calibrating on validation therefore uses only the past.
label and attack are EVALUATION ONLY. Never an input.
Endpoints are keyed on the flow's FIRST CAPTURED PACKET, not the flow record's src/dst, which disagree on 11.2-33.5% of rows depending on the day.
input.columns_verified: all 14 columns of event_latents.parquet are listed above and exist; checked against the real schema on 2026-09-20

key.link: directed pair sender->receiver. 237,293 keys on the Bot 3M slice. Detection only: an attacker/victim link carries NO benign traffic (90,039 events, zero benign), so there are zero early positives BY CONSTRUCTION and anticipation cannot be measured on it.
key.sender: source host. 15,174 keys. THE ANTICIPATION KEY - a host emits benign traffic before it attacks and that precursor is learnable.
key.receiver: destination host. 9,733 keys. Rejected: recall_early 0.14-0.31 and unstable across seeds. Being attacked is not a property of the victim's own traffic.

target_definitions.horizon: H is in EVENTS, not seconds. H=20 on a sender key spans a median 16 s but 0.36 s at p10 and 289 s at p90. Always report wall-clock lead beside it.
target_definitions.coming_attack: for each event: is any of the next H events on the same key an attack
target_definitions.onset: the first attack event of a campaign on a key - its first attack, or the first after a benign gap
target_definitions.early_positive: a BENIGN event that has an attack coming on its key within H. This is what recall_early is measured on.

must_emit.per_family: one calibrated probability per family per horizon, benign first, matching models.detector.head.family_codes so both arms name families identically
must_emit.never: a binary attack/no-attack decision. Block 12 maps your output to kill-chain stages and cannot do that without a family. Emit probabilities and let the serving path threshold them.
must_emit.state_metadata_why: an alert on a cold-started key is weaker evidence than one on a warm key, and nothing currently distinguishes them

acceptance_criteria.measured_on: 3M-event slice of Friday-02-03-2018 centred on Bot, sender key, 2 seeds, deterministic

onsets_caught_early.bar: >= 275, BUT read onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns first. Under the current K=1 definition these are attack RESUMPTIONS about 2 s after a benign blip, not campaign starts. Matching 275/291 says your model detects resumption as well as the proxy does; it says nothing about anticipating a campaign. Report the stricter K>=H definition alongside it - on Bot that count is ZERO in test, which is the honest number.

measured_lead.bar: NOT a bar on this target - the data contains at most 2.0 s of lead on the sender key (see lead_time_the_truth). Do not try to beat it by changing the objective. If you want lead, propose a different TARGET - time-based horizon or campaign-level - and say so before building.

settled_by_measurement.state: one per key, never one over the stream - global reached recall 0.29 where per-key reached 0.83+
settled_by_measurement.chunk_width_why: a hub node carries thousands of events and a wide chunk answers all of them from one stale state: receiver-keyed recall 0.108 at window 4096 against 0.930 at 512. 512 is also Block 8's live batch, so training and serving see the same staleness. Do not tune them apart.
settled_by_measurement.rollout: iterate the dynamics, feeding the model's own predicted observation back in. Separate heads per horizon score the same (0.998 vs 0.9976) while never learning a transition.
settled_by_measurement.training: one step at a time, roll forward only at inference. Backpropagating through 50 unrolled steps is expensive and unstable.
settled_by_measurement.fusion: flow records enter at Block 8 as their own message kind, union-merged with a presence bit. Late concatenation of separately trained latents was worse on false alarms, calibration and skill.

traps.scatter_nondeterminism: scatter_ with duplicate indices has no defined winner - 16 distinct results in 200 repeats on one real chunk. It masqueraded as ~5 points of seed variance and produced three findings that collapsed once fixed. Use scatter_reduce_(reduce='amax'). Test by scoring a prefix and requiring bit-identical results.
traps.effective_sample_size: the 320 early positives sit on 9 hosts. n is hosts, not events.
traps.intensity_confound: attacking hosts emit 2,582 events/hour against a median of 1.9 - a 1,400x outlier - and per-key score normalisation was 40x WORSE, which says the signal lives in a host's score level. Your generalisation may be generalisation of 'very busy host'.
traps.calibration_source: validation alone beat validation+train on this slice (1.112% vs 1.300% realised against a 1% budget) because splits are time-ordered and validation sits nearest test. The detection arm measured the opposite on its subsets. Re-measure per arm, do not inherit.
traps.densified_ids: If you write your own loader: densify sender and receiver ids TOGETHER or keep them raw. The proxy's load_latents densifies them separately, so a host ends up with different ids in the two roles and cross-role comparisons silently break. It cost us a wrong 'no chain exists' result.
traps.seed_agreement: does not validate anything - both seeds shared the scatter_ bug and agreed with disjoint ranges.
traps.dataset_artefacts: four Infiltration hosts 'dwelled' 4.266/4.273/4.254/4.271 h before attacking. That is the scenario script, not behaviour. Suspiciously equal numbers are usually the dataset.

untested: multi-class family prediction: the PROXY implements it, but every run used a single-family slice where it collapses to binary, so you inherit an UNVERIFIED design decision. Thursday-15 (DoS-GoldenEye 41,508 + DoS-Slowloris 11,111) is the cheapest real test.
a live runner: every 'live' number is an offline replay with live rules imposed.

required.data/latents/<run>/<day>/latents_manifes: READ FIRST. day, n_events, event_latent_dim, arm, observation_budget_ms, ordering, endpoint semantics. Tells you what to expect before you open the parquet.
required.data/latents/<run>/<day>/event_latents.p: your main input: one row per event with packets, in availability order. Columns under 'input.columns'.
required.data/events/<day>/node_index.parquet: node_id -> ip, first_seen_t, n_events. You need this to turn a key back into a host for any output a person reads, and to see how skewed the traffic is (median host 7 lifetime events, attacking hosts ~9,700).

optional.data/model_cache/context/<run>/best.pt: the frozen Block 8 that produced the context. Needed only to RE-EXPORT (see below).
optional.data/model_cache/block9/<run>/best.pt: the frozen Block 9 that produced z. Needed only to RE-EXPORT (see below).
optional.data/model_cache/context/<run>/history.c: Block 8's training curve, for the per-block metric (val link PR-AUC) that sits beside your results.

never_an_input.data/events/<day>/events.parquet: the raw event stream; Blocks 7-9 already consumed it. Reading it directly risks using fields the 10 ms verdict never saw.

re_export_explained.what_it_means: regenerating event_latents.parquet yourself instead of using the one handed to you. It RE-RUNS the frozen Blocks 8 and 9 over a day's events and writes a fresh parquet.
when_you_would: you want a different day or slice than the one exported (e.g. Thursday-15 for the two-family test, or a full day)
you want a different arm: packets only versus packets + CICFlowMeter records
the export went stale because Blocks 8 or 9 were retrained upstream
you want different contents, e.g. Block 8's s (100 wide) instead of Block 9's z (32 wide), to see what the compression costs you
re_export_explained.CRITICAL: re-export means re-RUNNING, never re-TRAINING. --block8 and --load both point at existing checkpoints. If you retrain Blocks 8 or 9 the z space changes, and every threshold, every acceptance criterion in this file, and the Block 13 baseline comparison all become invalid - you would be measuring against numbers produced by a different representation. Retraining is Kaustuk's side of the boundary.
re_export_explained.command: uv run python -m models.compressor --encoder mlp --block8 <block8>/best.pt --out <block9> --load <block9>/best.pt --days <day> --events 3000000 --family Bot --export data/latents/<run>

example.description: one row of event_latents.parquet and what a correct Block 10 does with it
what_block10_does: read state[1622] as it stood BEFORE this chunk of 512 events
roll the dynamics forward 20 steps from that state, feeding the model's own predicted z back in
read the class head at each step -> p_k per family
P(Bot within 20 events on host 1622) = 1 - prod_k (1 - p_k[Bot])
emit that probability plus lead_events and lead_seconds; do NOT threshold it yourself
fold this row's z into state[1622] for the next chunk
example.note: this row is benign and its host attacks within 20 events, so it is an EARLY POSITIVE - the population recall_early is measured on. There are 320 of them on 9 hosts in this slice.

source_of_truth.family codes: models.detector.head.family_codes - benign is 0, family k is families[k-1]; use the same order
source_of_truth.z width: 32, stated as event_latent_dim in latents_manifest.json - read it rather than hard-coding

the_proxy.where: models/world_model_proxy/model.py, ~75,000 parameters. You are REPLACING this file, not extending it.
read_it_for: how the per-key state table and its LRU eviction are done
how the rollout iterates the dynamics rather than using a head per horizon
how coming_attack / onsets / next_on_link define the targets - reuse these definitions so your numbers are comparable to the baseline
the metric set in run(): recall_early, onsets_caught_early, next-state skill, ECE
the_proxy.run_it_once_to: establish the baseline on YOUR machine before you replace it, so the comparison is on the same hardware and the same data rather than against numbers from someone else's run
baseline_commands: uv run python -m models.world_model_proxy.model --latents data/latents/f_norec_s0/Friday-02-03-2018 --window 512 --seed 0 --key link sender receiver
uv run python tools/world_model/alert_economics.py --latents data/latents/f_norec_s0/Friday-02-03-2018 --key sender
uv run python tools/world_model/leave_attackers_out.py --latents data/latents/f_norec_s0/Friday-02-03-2018 --key sender
reuse_directly: tools/world_model/alert_economics.py - the recall/alert-rate curve and incident collapse
tools/world_model/fpr_levers.py - threshold, gate, persistence, per-key normalisation compared
tools/world_model/leave_attackers_out.py - the generalisation test your model must also pass
the_proxy.note: these tools read event_latents.parquet, not models/world_model_proxy/model.py's model, so they keep working against whatever you build as long as you emit a per-event score.

how_to_calculate.test_window_hours: hours = (max(t_obs[test]) - min(t_obs[test])) / 3600. On the Bot 3M slice this is 0.715 h. Every per-hour figure divides by it, so quote it beside any rate.
how_to_calculate.recall: TP / (TP + FN) over TEST rows only, where a positive is an event whose target is true.
how_to_calculate.recall_early: TP_early / P_early, where P_early = TEST rows that are BENIGN and have an attack coming on their key within H. This is the anticipation number. On the Bot sender key P_early = 320.
how_to_calculate.recall_ongoing: TP_ongoing / P_ongoing over TEST rows that are THEMSELVES attacks with more attack following. P_ongoing = 16,379, so pooled recall is 98% this number - never report recall alone.
how_to_calculate.fpr: FP / N_negatives over TEST rows. N_negatives = 558,522 on the Bot 3M slice.
how_to_calculate.false_incidents_per_hour: collapse alerts first, then divide. Collapse = group alerts by key, sort by time, and start a new incident whenever the gap to the previous alert on that key exceeds gap_seconds. An incident is TRUE if ANY alert inside it was a true positive, FALSE otherwise. Example: 30 alerts -> 8 false incidents -> 8 / 0.715 = 11.2/hour. The gap is a choice with a real cost: 1.81x collapse at 10 s, 3.42x at 60 s, 5.91x at 300 s.
how_to_calculate.onsets_caught_early: count of campaign ONSETS in test that had an alert fire strictly before them. An onset is the first attack event of a campaign on a key - its first attack, or the first after a benign gap. Each campaign contributes exactly one, so unlike recall_early this cannot be inflated by one long campaign. Bot sender key: 291 onsets in test.
how_to_calculate.lead_events / lead_seconds: for each alert that precedes an attack on its key: lead_events = the number of events between them; lead_seconds = t_obs(attack) - t_obs(alert). Report the MEDIAN and p90 of both. Measured: 1 event and 2.02 s at BOTH median and p90.
how_to_calculate.probability_within_H: from the rollout, per family f: P(f within H) = 1 - prod over k=1..H of (1 - p_k[f]), where p_k = softmax(head(state after k imagined steps)). Compute in log space: 1 - exp(sum_k log(1 - p_k[f])) - the direct product underflows.
how_to_calculate.ece: Expected Calibration Error. Bin predictions by predicted probability (15 bins). In each bin b compute |mean(predicted) - fraction(actually happened)|. ECE = sum_b (n_b / N) * that gap. 0 is perfect. Read it as: at ECE 0.002, a stated 3% happens 3% +/- 0.2 percentage points of the time.
how_to_calculate.brier: mean((predicted probability - outcome)^2) over TEST rows. Lower is better; it penalises both miscalibration and poor discrimination, where ECE sees only miscalibration.
how_to_calculate.next_state_skill_vs_persistence: 1 - MSE(model) / MSE(persistence), where persistence predicts z_next = z_now on the same key. 0 = no better than assuming nothing changes; 1 = perfect; NEGATIVE = worse than doing nothing, which is what a broken design looks like. Always report the persistence MSE beside it - a raw MSE means nothing alone.
how_to_calculate.persistence_rule (persist-k): alert only when k CONSECUTIVE events on the same key exceed the threshold. Keep a counter per key; increment on an event above threshold, RESET TO ZERO on any event below it; fire when the counter reaches k. Measured at k=3: false alarms 58 -> 30 with recall_early and onsets unchanged.
how_to_calculate.threshold_from_budget: threshold = quantile(scores of CALIBRATION rows that are negative, 1 - budget). Calibration rows are validation only by default - measured better than validation+train on this data (1.112% vs 1.300% realised against a 1% budget) because splits are time-ordered and validation sits nearest test.
how_to_calculate.threshold_from_precision_floor: walk the precision-recall curve on calibration rows and take the HIGHEST-RECALL threshold whose precision reaches the floor. Equivalent in outcome to a budget but stated in terms an operator can agree to. Measured: precision>=0.999 landed on the same point as a 3e-5 budget.

definitions_from_code.end: t + Flow Duration, i.e. the flow's LAST packet
definitions_from_code.t_obs: min(t + 0.010, end) - models/data/prefix.py. The verdict moment. A flow that finishes inside the budget is scored when it finishes, not at t+10 ms.
definitions_from_code.observation_population: COMPLETED if end <= t + 0.010, else EARLY - same file, same line
definitions_from_code.flow_time (kind 2): t + iat_mean * max(pkt_n - 1, 0) - models/context_encoder/data.py. The moment the K-th packet lands, derived because exporting exact per-packet times would mean re-reading every packet of every day. Checked against real packet times on 200,000 events: median difference 0.2 ns, worst 8.3 us, which is float32 in the stored aggregates.
definitions_from_code.record_time (kind 3): t + Flow Duration - models/context_encoder/records.py. This is the EARLIEST the record can exist, not when it is emitted.

CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.the_error: earlier versions of this contract said the record arrives 'a median 106 s after the verdict' as if always. It does not.
CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.why: record_time == end, and for a COMPLETED_BEFORE_BUDGET flow t_obs == end too - so the record's earliest existence time EQUALS the verdict time for those flows.

measured_on_Thursday_15.Benign: 54.9% of records land after the verdict, median lag 2.2 s, p90 115.9 s

CORRECTION_records_are_not_always_late.so: roughly 45% of benign records are available at the verdict moment. The 106 s figure is the median lag among SLOWLORIS records that are late - the worst case, not the typical one.

timing_and_availability.LIVE_emission_time: record_time is a floor. CICFlowMeter emits at flow close or at its idle/active timeout, which is at or after t + Flow Duration. Stamp kind 3 with YOUR ACTUAL emission time and deliver in that order. Do not back-date it to t + Flow Duration - that would claim the record existed before you had it.
timing_and_availability.the_rule_that_still_holds: a flow's own kind-3 record must never inform that flow's own 10 ms verdict. Block 8 queues messages and applies them at the START of the next batch, so a record whose availability time equals t_obs reaches memory one batch later and cannot affect its own event. Preserve that: queue, then apply on the next batch boundary.
timing_and_availability.two_verdicts: stage='observation' at t_obs, and stage='flow_close' when the record lands. For a completed_before_budget flow these can be close together or simultaneous in time, but they are still two separate rows with their own timestamps.

statistics_you_must_report.why: report these and the comparison to the proxy is direct. Omit one and it is not.
statistics_you_must_report.required_per_key: report link, sender AND receiver. They answer different questions and dropping one hides a regression - link cannot measure anticipation at all, and receiver is where records look unstable.
statistics_you_must_report.required_per_horizon: H = 5, 20 and 50. Reporting one horizon hides whether the rollout is doing anything.
statistics_you_must_report.required_seeds: at least 2 full runs, and report the RANGE not the mean. Three of our findings died to a second seed.

must_also_report.prefix_invariance: score a prefix of the stream, compare to the same rows in the full run, report the max absolute difference. Must be exactly 0.
must_also_report.label_permutation: permute the training labels, retrain, report recall and recall_early on true test labels. Must collapse to about 0.
must_also_report.leave_attackers_out: 3 folds over the attacking hosts, report recall_early and onsets on HELD-OUT hosts only.
must_also_report.persistence_baseline: always report next_state_mse_persistence beside next_state_mse. A raw MSE means nothing alone, and the skill score went NEGATIVE when our design was broken.

statistics_you_must_report.do_not_report_alone: pooled recall. 16,379 of 16,699 positives are ongoing attacks, so it is 98% a detection number and says almost nothing about anticipation.

lead_time_the_truth.headline: The ~2 second lead is a property of the TARGET DEFINITION, not of the model or the training objective. Measured 2026-09-20 as ground truth, with no model involved.
lead_time_the_truth.what_was_measured: for every benign TEST event on a host that ever attacks, the unbounded time until that host's next attack - no horizon cap at all
lead_time_the_truth.therefore: the maximum warning available ANYWHERE in this data on the sender key is 2.0 seconds. No training objective can produce lead the data does not contain.
lead_time_the_truth.why_the_data_is_like_this: an attacking host emits 2,582 events/hour against a median host's 1.9, so its benign traffic is interleaved with its attack traffic at sub-second spacing. 'A benign event on an attacking host' is almost by definition adjacent to an attack. A target phrased as 'attack within H EVENTS on this key' can therefore never span more than a couple of seconds on a busy host.
lead_time_the_truth.what_we_tried_and_abandoned: a lead-rewarding objective (--lead-steps: roll the dynamics forward during training and supervise each rolled step against the class at that distance). Implemented and tested, then ABANDONED once the ground-truth measurement above showed there is nothing for it to learn. The flag remains in models/world_model_proxy/model.py; it is not a defect, it simply cannot help on this target.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.PRINCIPLE: the rollout predicts STATE -> NEXT STATE. A step is one more event on the key, not a tick of a clock. PREDICT in state transitions; REPORT in seconds. Reporting lead_seconds beside lead_events is right and necessary for an operator; phrasing the TARGET in seconds is not, because it would force the rollout to additionally predict inter-event gaps - a different and harder model that breaks the transition framing.
WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.rejected_time_based_horizon: 'attack within T SECONDS on this key' was proposed and WITHDRAWN. It asks the rollout to answer in units it does not operate in. Keep the horizon in events.

still_open_campaign_level.target: will this host attack at all - the state of a host BEFORE it has ever attacked
still_open_campaign_level.why_it_stays_state_shaped: still per-event, still 'what comes next'. Only the label changes.
still_open_campaign_level.the_lead_it_could_offer: whatever traffic precedes a host's FIRST attack. Unmeasured until now - the 2.0 s ceiling was measured on benign events that have a LATER attack, which is a different population from events before the first one.

still_open_cross_host.target: host A is attacking - is host B next
still_open_cross_host.why_it_stays_state_shaped: it is a GRAPH rollout, not a time one: the state of A conditioning the state of B. Block 8 already carries that structure - per-link memory plus neighbourhood attention over recent peers - so the machinery exists.
still_open_cross_host.the_lead_it_could_offer: the stagger between hosts' first attacks. Topology being a star does NOT rule this out - that conflates topology with timing. If the 10 Bot hosts start at staggered times, the stagger is real lead regardless of them all hitting one hub.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CREATE LEAD.why_the_2s_ceiling_is_not_a_units_proble: on an attacking host, benign traffic does not precede attacks by much - measured max 2.0 s unbounded. Re-expressing the same target in seconds cannot create positives that do not exist. The lead has to come from a DIFFERENT KEY or a DIFFERENT POINT IN THE CAMPAIGN.

lead_time_the_truth.correction_note: earlier versions of these documents called the lead 'the biggest capability gap' and told the Block 10 owner to fix the objective. That was wrong and would have wasted his time. The gap is real but it is a TARGET design question, and on this dataset it may be unanswerable.

onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.headline: What this project has been calling a 'campaign onset' is mostly an ATTACK RESUMPTION about 2 seconds after a brief benign blip, not the start of a campaign. Measured 2026-09-20.
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.the_definition_in_code: models.world_model_proxy.model.onsets marks an attack event whose PREVIOUS EVENT ON THAT KEY was not an attack. On a host whose benign and attack traffic interleave at sub-second spacing, that fires constantly.
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.stricter_definitions: requiring K consecutive non-attack events on the key before the attack: K=1 gives 1,565 onsets (291 in test), K=2 gives 135 (22 in test), K=5 gives 27 (1 in test), K=10 gives 15 (ZERO in test), K=20 gives 11 (ZERO in test).
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.the_11_real_campaign_starts: all 11 Bot hosts begin attacking between t=1520003454.1 and t=1520003455.0 - within 0.9 seconds of each other, a scripted simultaneous launch - and ALL 11 fall in the TRAIN split. There is no genuine campaign onset in the test split at all.
consequences: '275/291 onsets caught early' and '1,565/1,565 campaigns alerted' are real counts of attack RESUMPTION, not of campaign anticipation. Relabel them.
recall_early 0.9969 remains literally true, on 320 benign events whose attack is at most 2.0 s away.
cross-host lead on Bot is ~0.9 s, not hours: all hosts launch simultaneously, so 'A is attacking, is B next' has essentially nothing to predict on this day.
campaign-level lead is unmeasurable on Bot: the 11 real starts are all in train.
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.what_survives_untouched: detection. 99% recall at 1-2 false alarms, PR-AUC 1.0000 against the Block 13 baseline's 0.9259, and the baseline's collapse to recall 0.0003 at tight thresholds. That is a per-event claim and none of this bears on it.
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.how_to_report_it_honestly: report BOTH: (a) resumption-level onsets under the current K=1 definition, labelled as resumptions; and (b) genuine campaign starts, defined as requiring at least H non-attack events on the key, with the count in each split stated. On Bot (b) is zero in test, and saying so is the honest result.
onsets_are_resumptions_not_campaigns.open: whether any other day differs is measured by tools/measure/lead_ceiling_days.py, queued 2026-09-20. Bot alone cannot settle it.

checkpointing.status: DONE -- world_model.py previously wrote only a CSV and had no save/load at all
checkpointing.save: models/world_model_proxy/model.py --save PATH (one file per latents directory and key)
checkpointing.load: models/world_model_proxy/model.py --load PATH evaluates saved weights and trains nothing
checkpointing.contents: dynamics weights, the latent scaler (z_mean/z_std fitted on the train split), family names, the key, window, budget, the per-horizon thresholds, and the warm per-key state table
checkpointing.why_the_scaler: run() standardises z with the training split's mean and std. A reloaded checkpoint that standardises differently scores on a different scale and every threshold is void
checkpointing.verified: reloading reproduces recall, precision, fpr, brier, ece and next_state_mse identically on Thursday-15, and skips training (48 s against 81 s)
checkpointing.state_table_caveat: the table is indexed by node ids, and node ids are PER DAY (data/events/<day>/node_index.parquet is built one day at a time). Slot i is a different host on a different day, so restore_state defaults to False. A live deployment needs its own stable ip -> id map before a warm restart is meaningful

still_untested.multi_class: NO LONGER UNTESTED -- run on Thursday-15 (DoS-GoldenEye + DoS-Slowloris) on 2026-09-20: recall 0.772 at H=5, 0.701 at H=20, realised FPR 2.31% against a 1% budget (2.3x overshoot, against the detection arm's 1.0-1.8x). Brier 0.0158, ECE 0.0163, next-state skill vs persistence +0.185
still_untested.anticipation: BLOCKED, and not by the model. segment_split cuts 60/10/30 inside every attack window and benign stretch separately, so splits interleave in wall-clock time: 1,677,561 of 1,680,628 test benign rows on the Bot day occur BEFORE the latest train attack. Any 'will this host attack later' score is therefore contaminated. The lead is real in the data (Bot: 2,568 test rows across 10 hosts whose first attack is still ahead, ~44 min median) but only cross-day transfer or tools/world_model/leave_attackers_out.py can score it

runtime.configure: models.runtime.configure() -- reproducible by default; the world-model proxy already calls it
runtime.torch_compile: the one place in this repository where it is likely to pay is your per-chunk training step: many small ops (GRUCell, two linears) repeated thousands of times, which is exactly the shape torch.compile is built for. It is unmeasured here because no C compiler is installed. Use models.runtime.maybe_compile so a missing compiler degrades to eager instead of failing mid-run
runtime.determinism: do not enable fast=True while measuring. A scatter_ with duplicate indices once produced 16 distinct results in 200 repeats here and invalidated three claims; TF32 and cudnn autotuning are the same class of problem

explainability.what: the attention distribution over each event's neighbourhood, which the context encoder computes and used to discard. Turn it on with encoder.explain = True
explainability.guarantee: verified to leave the encoding bit-identical, so enabling explainability cannot change a verdict
explainability.care: an event with an empty neighbourhood attends a zeroed dummy slot; its weights are an artefact. top_neighbours reports -1 for those rather than presenting padding as evidence
